summary: UCSB revises three earlier specifications. Support for the Online System network interface in RFC 74 was dropped because no site had used it. The remote job entry specification in RFC 105 no longer uses a message type byte. The file system specification in RFC 122 is also revised, in line with new host-host protocol changes.

eli5.summary: A university tidies its old instruction sheets. One is thrown out because nobody used it, and the others are updated to match new network rules.

subtitle: A 1971 UCSB note that retires one network service and adjusts two others to match protocol changes.

tldr.problem: Three UCSB network specifications (RFC 74, RFC 105 and RFC 122) no longer matched reality after changes to the Host-Host protocol and a lack of users.
tldr.mechanism: This note lists four revisions: RFC 74 is declared obsolete, the message type is dropped from RJE and RJOR, their listening sockets change, and byte sizes are fixed for the user connection.
tldr.outcome: It updates RFC 105 and RFC 122 and marks RFC 74 as obsolete. The RFC itself is a short change notice, not a full protocol.

today: RFC 217 updates RFC 105 and RFC 122 and declares RFC 74 obsolete. Its status is listed as Unknown.

sections.title: Three Documents Being Revised
sections.content:
RFC 217, written by James E. White at the University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB), revises three earlier UCSB documents. They cover the On-Line System (OLS) in RFC 74, Remote Job Entry (RJE) and Remote Job Output Retrieval (RJOR) in RFC 105, and the Simple-Minded File System (SMFS) in RFC 122.

The note is dated 8 September 1971 and lists four numbered revisions.
sections.eli5: It is a short note saying which of three old instruction sheets are out of date and what to change in them.

sections.title: The Four Revisions
sections.content:
First, no network site is known to have written code for the OLS software documented in RFC 74. UCSB therefore stopped supporting it, and RFC 74 is declared obsolete.

Second, following Host-Host protocol changes, the notion of message type is dropped from RJE and RJOR. They no longer send, or expect to receive, 8 bits of zeros as the first byte on a connection.

Third, RJE and RJOR now use a standard ICP (initial connection protocol) to create a full duplex connection to the user. They listen on sockets x'201' and x'301' instead of x'200' and x'300'. RJOR still calls the user back over a simplex connection to the user's receive socket when requested output is ready.
sections.eli5: One service is closed because nobody used it. The job services get new mailbox numbers and stop sending a pointless first byte.

sections.title: Byte Sizes
sections.content: RJE/RJOR and SMFS specify a byte size of eight for their connection to the user's receive socket. The user may choose the byte size of the other simplex connection. UCSB accepts any valid byte size there.
sections.eli5: On the connection that carries data to you, the pieces must be eight bits wide. On the other one you can pick the size you like.
